lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I should be ranked above you, Libyan. I'm the better man.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: On the contrary. I am.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Fine. Let Minos decide.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: [sighs] And who are you two?
lines.description: weary judge, already over the docket

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: This is Hannibal, the Carthaginian. I am Alexander, son of Philip.
lines.description: formal introduction, stressing his own name

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Good heavens — both distinguished. So what's the quarrel about?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Precedence. He claims he was a better general than I was. Whereas I — as everyone knows — surpassed in warfare not just him, but practically everyone who came before me.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Right. Each of you speak in turn. You first, Libyan.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: One advantage I've gained from being down here, Minos, is that I've picked up Greek. So he can't even claim the upper hand on that. Now: I say the men most deserving of praise are those who began as nothing and rose to greatness by their own efforts — men who built up power and proved themselves worthy of rule. Take me. I set out for Spain with a handful of men, as my brother's subordinate, and was judged worthy of the supreme command. I took the Celtiberians, crushed the western Gauls, crossed the great mountains, overran everything around the Po, sacked city after city, subdued the Italian plain, and reached the very suburbs of the leading city. In a single day I killed so many that their rings had to be measured out in bushels, and we bridged rivers with the corpses.
lines.description: controlled rhetoric, underdog pride gathering force

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: And all of this I did without calling myself the son of Ammon, without pretending to be a god, without trotting out my mother's dreams. I admitted I was a man. I was matched against the cleverest generals and grappled with the most warlike soldiers — I wasn't beating up Medes and Armenians who run before they're chased and hand over the victory to anyone who has the nerve to come at them.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: Alexander inherited his father's kingdom and expanded it — far, yes — but riding the wave of Fortune. And once he'd won, once he'd beaten that disaster Darius at Issus and Arbela, he abandoned his ancestral ways: demanded to be worshipped, went native on Median customs, butchered his friends at dinner parties, had them arrested and executed. I, by contrast, governed my country as an equal among equals. When the enemy launched a great fleet against Libya and my country summoned me home, I obeyed at once, presented myself as a private citizen, and when I was condemned, I bore it with good grace. And I did all this as a barbarian, with no Greek education — not reciting Homer like this fellow, not raised at the knee of Aristotle the sophist — with nothing but my own natural ability. These are the grounds on which I claim to be the better man. If he's the prettier, because he tied a diadem round his head — well, that may impress Macedonians, but it hardly makes him superior to a brave and capable general who relied on judgment rather than luck.
lines.description: sustained forensic heat, ending with dry disdain

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Not a bad speech — and rather better than you'd expect from a Libyan pleading his own case. And you, Alexander? What's your reply?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I oughtn't to dignify a man this insolent with any reply at all, Minos. My reputation alone should be enough to inform you what sort of king I was, and what sort of brigand he was. Still — consider whether I outstripped him by a little. I was still young when I came to power. I took hold of a kingdom in chaos. I hunted down my father's murderers. I terrified Greece by destroying Thebes, was elected commander by the Greeks themselves — and I wasn't content to nurse my Macedonian inheritance and rule only what my father left me. I conceived the whole world. I thought it intolerable not to master all of it. I led a small force into Asia, won a great battle at the Granicus, took Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia — sweeping up everything in my path — and arrived at Issus, where Darius was waiting with armies in the hundreds of thousands.
lines.description: proud, wounded majesty swelling into epic cadence

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And from then on, Minos — you people know how many dead I sent down to you in a single day. The ferryman says his boat couldn't handle them: most of them had to lash together rafts and paddle across. And I did this leading from the front, taking the wounds myself. I won't bore you with Tyre, or Arbela — I reached India, I made the Ocean the boundary of my empire, I captured their elephants, I subdued Porus. I crossed the Tanais and beat the Scythians — not a people to be sneezed at — in a great cavalry battle. I did well by my friends and made my enemies pay. And if men took me for a god, you can forgive them — the scale of what I did rather invited the conclusion.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And in the end — I died a king. He died a fugitive, hiding with Prusias the Bithynian, which was exactly what he deserved, being the most treacherous and savage of men. I won't even mention how he conquered Italy — not by strength, but by villainy, perfidy, and trickery. Nothing lawful, nothing in the open. And as for his sneer about my luxury — he seems to have forgotten his own performance at Capua, our remarkable hero lounging about with courtesans and frittering away the campaigning season. As for me — if I hadn't decided the West was beneath my attention and turned east instead, what great achievement would there have been in taking Italy without spilling a drop of blood, and rolling up Libya and everything as far as Cadiz? They weren't worth fighting — they were already cowering, already calling me master. I've said my piece. Pass judgment, Minos. That's more than enough out of much that could be said.
lines.description: scornful and expansive, ending with imperious finality

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: Not yet — not until you've heard me too.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: And who might you be, my good man? Where do you hail from?

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: Scipio, the Italian general. The one who brought down Carthage and beat the Libyans in great battles.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Well then. What have you to say?

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: That I am Alexander's inferior — but Hannibal's superior, since I defeated him, chased him down, and forced him into ignominious flight. So how is this man not shameless, contending with Alexander, when I — Scipio, the man who beat him — don't even presume to put myself in the same bracket?
lines.description: elegant self-deprecation with a precise sting

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: [chuckles] By Zeus, Scipio, that's handsomely put. Very well. First place: Alexander. Second: you. And then, if you like, third: Hannibal — who isn't to be sniffed at either.
lines.description: amused judgment, briskly deflating the contest
